questions.prompt: Phase 4 "changes the direction of trust" in grouphelpdesk. What did the API accept before, why was that unsafe, what is the new flow from credentials to the services, how is a ticket's creator set now (and what happens to a createdBy the client still sends), and how does the guide define authentication versus authorization?

keyPoints.text: Before Phase 4 the API accepted identity fields such as createdBy, authorId, actorId and viewerRole from the browser.
keyPoints.quote:
the API accepted fields like `createdBy`, `authorId`,
`actorId`, and `viewerRole` from the browser.

keyPoints.text: Trusting client-sent identity fields lets the caller choose who the server acts as, because a user can open dev tools and send any JSON they want.
keyPoints.quote:
A user can open dev
tools and send any JSON they want.

keyPoints.text: New flow, step one: the client sends credentials, the server verifies them and issues a token.
keyPoints.quote: client sends credentials -> server verifies credentials -> server issues token

keyPoints.text: Step two: the client sends the token, the server derives the current user, and services use that user.
keyPoints.quote: client sends token -> server derives current user -> services use current user

keyPoints.text: The ticket controller sets createdBy from req.currentUser!.id.
keyPoints.quote: createdBy: req.currentUser!.id;

keyPoints.text: A createdBy sent by the client is ignored on authenticated routes.
keyPoints.quote:
The client may still send `createdBy`, but the
server ignores it for authenticated routes.

keyPoints.text: Authentication answers who is making the request; authorization answers whether that user may do this action.
keyPoints.quote: Authorization answers: "Is this user allowed to do this action?"

questions.prompt: Trace a grouphelpdesk login and a later authenticated request: what the login endpoint does and returns, where the frontend keeps the token and how it sends it (and that storage choice's trade-off), what the middleware attaches and which middlewares guard routes, what a 401 versus a 403 tells you, and how sessions expire and survive a restart in the current snapshot.

keyPoints.text: POST /api/auth/login finds the user by email, verifies the password with scrypt, and creates an opaque session token.
keyPoints.quote: verifies the password with `scrypt`, creates an opaque session token

keyPoints.text: It returns the token plus a safe user object.
keyPoints.quote:
returns
the token plus a safe user object.

keyPoints.text: The frontend keeps the token in localStorage and sends it as an Authorization: Bearer header.
keyPoints.quote: The frontend stores that token in `localStorage`

keyPoints.text: localStorage tokens are convenient for this learning app but carry XSS trade-offs.
keyPoints.quote:
They are convenient for this
  learning app, but have XSS tradeoffs.

keyPoints.text: optionalAuth reads the header, looks up the session and attaches req.currentUser; protected routes use requireAuth or requireRole.
keyPoints.quote:
`optionalAuth` reads the header, looks up the session, and attaches
`req.currentUser`.

keyPoints.text: A 401 means check the Authorization header and the stored token; a 403 means logged in but lacking a required role.
keyPoints.quote:
the user is logged in but does not have one of the
required roles for that route.

keyPoints.text: Login sets expiresAt from SESSION_TTL_HOURS and writes a Session row, so sessions expire and can survive a restart (the Session write is best-effort).
keyPoints.quote:
`login` sets `expiresAt` from
  `SESSION_TTL_HOURS` and writes a `Session` row

keyPoints.text: getCurrentUser checks the in-memory cache, then the database, and deletes expired sessions.
keyPoints.quote:
checks the in-memory cache first, then the database, and deletes expired
  sessions

questions.prompt: Beyond trusting client-sent identity fields, which auth mistakes does the grouphelpdesk guide warn about around password hashes, login error messages and where role checks live? Then, for the current snapshot, say how ticket reads are now scoped and which authorization and data-exposure gaps remain open (comments, user objects, the assign-ticket schema).

keyPoints.text: Never return passwordHash in login or user responses.
keyPoints.quote: Returning `passwordHash` in login or user responses.

keyPoints.text: Never reveal whether the email or the password was the wrong part of a login.
keyPoints.quote: Revealing whether the email or password was wrong during login.

keyPoints.text: Role checks only in controllers are not enough while services still accept unsafe actor IDs.
keyPoints.quote:
Adding role checks only in controllers while services still accept unsafe
    actor IDs.

keyPoints.text: Ticket reads are now scoped: customers and requesters see only their own tickets, and every viewer is limited to their organization.
keyPoints.quote:
Customers and requesters see only their own tickets,
  and every viewer is limited to their organization

keyPoints.text: Open gap: customers can still read and add public comments on any ticket.
keyPoints.quote:
Customers can read and add public
comments on any ticket

keyPoints.text: Open gap: although login returns a safe user, other endpoints (four in this snapshot) still return passwordHash inside user objects.
keyPoints.quote:
four endpoints return `passwordHash` inside user
objects.

keyPoints.text: assignTicketBodySchema still accepts actorId, though the client no longer sends it and the controller passes req.currentUser!.id instead.
keyPoints.quote: `assignTicketBodySchema` still accepts `actorId`
